lede: A table has no built-in order, so "the top five" or "newest first" only means something once you sort. `orderBy` sorts, `distinct` removes repeated rows and `limit` keeps the first few.
objectives: Sort rows with `orderBy` (or `sort`), ascending or descending
Break ties with a second sort column so the order is always the same
Remove repeated rows with `distinct` and count what's left
Get a top N with `orderBy` followed by `limit`, and say where missing values sort

blocks.md:
The tables above come from a small streaming service: `movies`, one row per film, and `ratings`, one row each time a member rated a film from 0.5 to 5.0 stars. On this page they're loaded as DataFrames with those names, and `F` is `pyspark.sql.functions`.

`df.orderBy("col")` gives back a **new** DataFrame with the same rows, sorted by that column, smallest first. To sort the other way, pass `F.desc("col")` or `F.col("col").desc()`. `sort` is the same method under another name.

blocks.title: Shortest and longest films first
blocks.code:
from pyspark.sql import functions as F

movies.orderBy("runtime_min").select("title", "runtime_min").show(3)

movies.orderBy(F.desc("runtime_min")).select("title", "runtime_min").show(3)
blocks.note: Ascending is the default. `F.desc` flips it, so the longest film comes first. `select` only trims what's printed; the sort keeps every column.

blocks.md: When two rows have the same value in the sort column, Spark may put them in **either** order, and it can change from one run to the next. Add a second column to decide ties. Each column can go its own way: here the newest year comes first, and within a year the titles go from A to Z.

blocks.title: Break ties with a second column
blocks.code:
from pyspark.sql import functions as F

by_year = movies.orderBy(F.desc("release_year"), "title")
by_year.select("title", "release_year").show()
blocks.note: Three films came out in 2024. Sorting by year alone would leave their order to chance; the title settles it.

blocks.md: `distinct()` keeps one copy of each row and drops the repeats. It compares **whole rows**, so `select` the columns you care about first. The rows come back in no particular order, so sort them afterwards if order matters.

blocks.title: The list of genres
blocks.code:
genres = movies.select("primary_genre").distinct()
genres.orderBy("primary_genre").show()

print(genres.count(), "genres")
print(movies.select("primary_genre", "language").distinct().count(), "genre and language pairs")
blocks.note: Ten films, eight genres: Drama and Thriller appear twice. With two columns, a row is a repeat only when both values match, so every film here is its own pair.

blocks.md: `limit(n)` keeps at most `n` rows. On its own it keeps whichever rows Spark reaches first, which isn't a top anything. **Sort first, then limit**, and include enough sort columns that ties are settled.

blocks.title: The three highest ratings
blocks.code:
from pyspark.sql import functions as F

top = ratings.orderBy(F.desc("rating"), "movie_id", "user_id").limit(3)
top.show()
blocks.note: Two ratings of 5.0 tie, and so do two of 4.5. `movie_id` and then `user_id` decide which come first, so the same three rows come back every time.

blocks.md: Missing values have a fixed place too: they come **first** when sorting ascending and **last** when sorting descending. To choose, use `asc_nulls_last()`, `asc_nulls_first()`, `desc_nulls_first()` or `desc_nulls_last()` on a column.

blocks.title: Where missing values go
blocks.code:
from pyspark.sql import functions as F

runtimes = spark.createDataFrame([("M01", 118), ("M02", None), ("M03", 92)], "movie_id STRING, runtime_min INT")

runtimes.orderBy("runtime_min").show()
runtimes.orderBy(F.col("runtime_min").asc_nulls_last()).show()
blocks.note: The missing runtime sorts before 92 at first. `asc_nulls_last()` keeps the order ascending but moves it to the end.

blocks.title: Forgetting the brackets on desc
blocks.code:
from pyspark.sql import functions as F

movies.orderBy(F.col("release_year").desc).show()
blocks.note: `desc` is a method, so it needs brackets: `F.col("release_year").desc()`. Without them `orderBy` gets the method itself instead of a column, and says so.

concept.prompt: `movies.limit(3)` runs without `orderBy`. Which three films do you get?
choices: The three films with the smallest movie_id
Whichever three rows Spark reaches first; there's no promise which
Three films picked at random on purpose
concept.why: A DataFrame has no order until you sort it. `limit` just stops after `n` rows, so sort first when you mean "top".

concept.prompt: A column has the values 3, missing and 1. In what order does `orderBy("v")` put them?
concept.why: Missing values come first when sorting ascending and last when sorting descending. `asc_nulls_last()` changes that.

choices: One row per different pair of genre and language
Only the pairs that appear once
concept.why: `distinct` compares whole rows. Two rows are repeats only when every column matches, so here each different genre and language pair stays once.

review: `df.orderBy("col")` sorts ascending; `F.desc("col")` or `F.col("col").desc()` sorts descending. `sort` is the same method.
Rows that tie on the sort columns can come back in any order. Add another column to settle ties.
Missing values sort first ascending and last descending; `asc_nulls_last()` and friends choose.
`distinct()` keeps one copy of each whole row. Select the columns you care about first, then sort if order matters.
`limit(n)` keeps at most `n` rows. For a top N, sort first, then limit.
